However, the play began to regain popularity with a revival at a small theater in Notting Hill in 1901, followed by a return to the West End in 1902 and Broadway revivals in 1902 and 1910. A significant turning point came in 1908 when Robert Ross edited a collected edition of Wilde's works, helping to restore his reputation. In 1909, Alexander staged a successful revival at the St James's Theatre, which ran for 316 performances and was praised by Max Beerbohm, who predicted it would become a classic.

Throughout the early 20th century, the play saw numerous revivals, with notable productions in 1913 and 1923. By the 1920s, there was a growing preference for setting the play in the 1890s, as critics argued that Wilde's wit was best supported by the atmosphere and fashion of his own time. Sir Nigel Playfair's 1930 production at the Lyric, Hammersmith, featured John Gielgud as Jack, and Gielgud later produced and starred in a 1939 production at the Globe (now the Gielgud) Theatre, which was highly acclaimed for its fidelity to Wilde's vision. This production continued through several seasons, even during and after World War II, and was attended by the King and Queen in 1946, further cementing its respectability.

As Wilde's works regained popularity, "The Importance of Being Earnest" became the most frequently produced play, and by its centenary, it was noted as the second most known and quoted play in English, following only "Hamlet." Notable productions in the latter half of the 20th century included Sir Peter Hall's 1982 National Theatre production with Judi Dench as Lady Bracknell and Nicholas Hytner's 1993 production at the Aldwych Theatre, which occasionally referenced the play's supposed gay subtext.

Innovative and diverse interpretations of the play continued into the 21st century. The Abbey Theatre in Dublin staged an all-male cast production in 2005, featuring a character portrayal of Oscar Wilde. The Melbourne Theatre Company also produced the play in 2011, with Geoffrey Rush as Lady Bracknell. Additionally, the Roundabout Theatre Company staged a Broadway revival in 2011, directed by and starring Brian Bedford as Lady Bracknell, which received three Tony Award nominations. The play's international appeal was further demonstrated by the British Theatre Playhouse, which showcased it in Singapore and London in the mid-2000s.

Although official approval was not granted until May 31, 1947, design work had already commenced, and construction of the prototype, designated as Tu-77, began in early May. To minimize production time, modifications to the standard Tu-2 were kept to a minimum. The fuselage was extended by 400 mm (16 in), and the height of the rear fuselage was increased by 300 mm (12 in). Additionally, the aircraft was equipped with a new tricycle undercarriage, where the main gear units retracted into the engine nacelles. The control system was revised, and trim tabs were added to the elevators to enhance stability and control. The wing and tail were strengthened to handle the new power and structural demands.
